pages.student_title: Mission San Fernando Rey de España
pages.subtitle: The seventeenth California mission, known for its long building of arches, built at the Native village of Achoicominga.
pages.founding_source_note: Fernandeño Tataviam Band of Mission Indians, "History"; California Missions Foundation, "San Fernando Rey."
pages.intro: Mission San Fernando Rey de España was the seventeenth California mission. Father Fermín Lasuén founded it in 1797 at a Native village called Achoicominga, north of Los Angeles. The mission is known for its Long Building, with a row of arches. The Native people who were brought there came from many villages. They lost their freedom and, later, all of their land.
story_paragraphs: Long before the mission, Native people lived in villages across four valleys north of Los Angeles. Each village led itself, with its own leaders and its own land. People married into other villages, so many of them spoke more than one language. One group of villages is known as the Tataviam.

On September 8, 1797, Father Fermín Lasuén founded Mission San Fernando Rey de España at the village of Achoicominga. It was the seventeenth California mission. It was named for Saint Ferdinand, a king of Spain who lived long ago.

People from many villages and several nations were brought to the mission. The Spanish called all of them Fernandeños, after the mission. Their tribe today, the Fernandeño Tataviam Band of Mission Indians, says the mission enslaved more than 3,000 of their ancestors.

The tribe says that families were separated and holy places were destroyed. People needed a priest's permission to leave, and they were punished for breaking the rules. Many died from sickness and hunger. Even so, people went on holding their ceremonies and respecting their own village leaders.
The mission grew rich from their work. It had 21,000 animals and 32,000 grapevines. From 1810 to 1822, workers built the Long Building, where the priests lived and travelers could rest.

In 1834, the government took the mission away from the Church. In the 1840s, some Fernandeño families were given ranch land by the Mexican government. They had about one tenth of the valley. But after California joined the United States, they lost that land in the courts. By 1900, they had none left.
The old adobe church was damaged by earthquakes, and in 1971 an earthquake ruined it. A copy was built in 1974.
Today, the Fernandeño Tataviam Band has more than 900 members. Most still live in their homeland, and the tribe works to care for its land and culture.

type_specific.native_peoples_and_history: This mission was built at Achoicominga, a Native village. The people brought to the mission came from the San Fernando, Santa Clarita, Simi, and Antelope Valleys. They included the Tataviam, some Chumash, and several other groups. Before the mission, there was no single chief over everyone. Each family line governed itself. The tribe says the mission meant enslavement, the breaking up of families, sickness, hunger, and the loss of land and freedom. Many place names in the valley today come from Native village names, such as Tujunga, Topanga, Cahuenga, and Pacoima. Three family lines lived through those years. Their descendants make up the Fernandeño Tataviam Band of Mission Indians. A park in the city of San Fernando honors one of their leaders, Captain Rogerio Rocha, who was forced off his land.
type_specific.mission_life: San Fernando was a ranch, a farm, and a workshop. Native workers made leather, saddles, shoes, candles, and soap. They pressed olives, made wine, wove cloth, and ground flour. The mission's blacksmiths were known for fine ironwork, and its goods were sold in the town of Los Angeles. In 1842, bits of gold were found stuck to an onion pulled from a mission field. That was six years before the famous Gold Rush.
type_specific.architecture: The Long Building is the real treasure here. It is 243 feet long and two stories tall, with a covered walkway of arches along the front. It is the largest building left from mission days here, and it has been called the largest adobe building in California. It has been repaired several times, most recently after an earthquake in 1994, when steel bars were put inside the walls. The church is different. The old church was finished in 1806, but the one you see is a copy built in 1974. A star-shaped fountain from the mission's old water system still stands across from the Long Building.

pages.student_title: Mission San Luis Rey de Francia
pages.subtitle: The eighteenth California mission and the largest of them all, built on the homeland of the Payómkawichum, or Luiseño, people.
pages.founding_source_note: California Missions Foundation, "San Luis Rey de Francía"; Toucan Valley fact card for Mission San Luis Rey de Francia.
pages.intro: Mission San Luis Rey de Francia was the eighteenth California mission. Father Fermín Lasuén founded it in 1798 on the homeland of the Payómkawichum people, whom the Spanish called Luiseños. It became the largest of all the missions and was called the "King of the Missions." The people who built it lost thousands of lives to sickness. They had to keep their language alive in secret.
story_paragraphs: The people of this land call themselves Payómkawichum. The name means "the People of the West." They have lived here for more than 10,000 years. They governed themselves, cared for the plants and animals through the seasons, and made stone tools, baskets, and pottery. They traded with other peoples along trails across Southern California. Their stories taught children how to live well.
On June 13, 1798, Father Fermín Lasuén founded Mission San Luis Rey de Francia. It was the eighteenth California mission. It was named for Saint Louis, a king of France who lived in the 1200s.
Lasuén put a priest named Antonio Peyri in charge. Father Peyri stayed for 34 years. The Spanish began calling the people San Luiseños, and later just Luiseños.

The mission grew larger than any other. By 1825, 2,869 Native people lived there. They cared for about 50,000 animals. From 1811 to 1815, Native workers did most of the hard labor of building a great church shaped like a cross.

The Pechanga Band of Indians tells what this time was like for their ancestors. The new foods were not as healthy as their own. Smallpox, measles, and other sicknesses spread. Within a few decades, several thousand Payómkawichum had died. Strict rules kept people apart by age and by whether they were boys or girls. Stories and ceremonies were lost, and the people spoke their own language only in secret.

In 1834, the government took the mission away from the Church. The people who were still living went back to small villages or started new ones. Later, soldiers camped in the empty mission, and the church dome fell in.
In 1892, Franciscan priests came back and began to rebuild, led by Father Joseph O'Keefe.
Today, the Payómkawichum are still here, in seven bands. One of them, the Pechanga Band, was forced from its village in 1875 and now lives on its own reservation nearby.

type_specific.native_peoples_and_history: This mission stands on the homeland of the Payómkawichum, "the People of the West." The Spanish name for them, Luiseño, comes from the mission. Before the mission, their way of life made sure that everyone had food and a place to live. Native people built the mission and did its work. Mission life brought strict rules, sickness, and the loss of land, language, and freedom. Several thousand people died. After the missions closed, things did not get easier. In 1875, ranchers and a sheriff's men forced the Payómkawichum of Temecula out of their village. Many moved to a valley beside a spring called Pecháa'a, which gave the Pechanga Band its name. In the mission cemetery, a memorial put up in 1830 honors the Luiseño people.
type_specific.mission_life: San Luis Rey was like a small town. Its main square of buildings was about 500 feet on each side. In front of the mission, wide steps led down to a sunken garden and a large open-air laundry, where spring water flowed and women washed clothes. In 1830, all the unmarried women had to live in sleeping rooms on one side of the square. Native workers farmed, herded, and built. Father Peyri planted the first pepper trees in California here, and one from 1830 is still growing.
type_specific.architecture: The church is the one built from 1811 to 1815. Its walls are adobe on the inside and fired brick on the outside, and they are five feet thick. The church is shaped like a cross, and over the middle is a wooden dome with windows that let in light. No other California mission has a dome like it. One bell tower, 75 feet tall, stands at a corner. A second tower was planned but never built. The dome fell in during the years the mission stood empty and was rebuilt in the 1890s. The painted designs on the walls inside are from mission days, though they have been painted over. Only twelve of the 32 arches along the front are left.

pages.subtitle: The nineteenth California mission, built in a valley of the Chumash people, where the Chumash uprising of 1824 began.
pages.founding_source_note: National Park Service, "Mission Santa Inés, CA"; Toucan Valley fact card for Mission Santa Inés.
pages.intro: Mission Santa Inés was the nineteenth California mission. Father Estévan Tápis founded it in 1804 in a valley of the Chumash people, between two older missions. It is named for Saint Agnes. In 1824, a soldier beat a Chumash man here, and the Chumash rose up at three missions. Today, the Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians lives close by and teaches its language to its children.
story_paragraphs: The Chumash have lived in the valleys and along the coast of this region for thousands of years. Their homeland covered about 7,000 square miles. Their society had chiefs, healers, and skilled craftspeople, and women could be leaders too.

By 1804, the two missions nearest this valley were crowded. So, on September 17, 1804, Father Estévan Tápis founded a new mission halfway between them. About 200 people came to the first Mass. He named the mission for Saint Agnes, a brave Roman girl who died for her faith long ago. It was the nineteenth California mission. By the end of that year, 112 Chumash people had been baptized. At its largest, in 1816, the mission had 786 Native people.

In 1812, an earthquake destroyed most of the church. A new church was dedicated on July 4, 1817. It still stands. Workers also laid clay pipes under the ground to bring water from the mountains several miles away.
After Mexico became free from Spain in 1821, things grew worse for the Chumash. They were made to work for the soldiers and were given only promises of pay.

In February 1824, a soldier at Santa Inés beat a Chumash man. The Chumash had had enough. They fought back, and fires burned many of the mission buildings. The uprising spread quickly to Mission La Purísima and Mission Santa Bárbara. It went on for several months. Peace came when the governor pardoned the Chumash who had taken part.
In the 1830s, the government took the mission away from the Church, and most of the Chumash left. Later, the first school in California for training priests opened here.
By 1900, the mission was falling apart. A priest named Alexander Buckler spent twenty years cleaning and repairing it.
The Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians lives nearby today. In 2008, the tribe started a program to teach Samala, its language. There is now a Samala dictionary.

type_specific.native_peoples_and_history: This mission stands on the homeland of the Chumash people. The Chumash of this valley speak a language called Samala. When the mission came, many were baptized and brought to live there. Mission life brought forced work, strict rules, sickness, and the loss of land and freedom. The Santa Ynez Band says that sickness from Europe was the main reason the number of Chumash fell so far, from about 22,000 before the Spanish came to fewer than 3,000 at the missions by 1831. In 1824, the Chumash resisted, starting here. Today, the Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians has a reservation near the mission. The tribe teaches basket weaving, old recipes, archery, and the Samala language. It says, "We have survived and thrived because of our strength as a tribe."
type_specific.mission_life: Chumash workers here were known for their leather and metal work. They made saddles trimmed with silver and candlesticks of copper and silver. Water from the mountains filled two large tanks and turned the wheels of a mill that ground corn and wheat. The mill was built in 1820 by Joseph Chapman, a sailor who had once come to California with a pirate. The mission was also a place of teaching, and it was sometimes called the "Mission of the Passes."
type_specific.architecture: The adobe church is the one dedicated in 1817, and the long building beside it is from mission days too. Much of the inside is the way it was. The tile floor is old, and so is a bowl for baptisms made of copper and zinc by Native craftsmen. The walls were painted in 1825 with designs you can still see. The bell wall is not the first one. It fell down in 1911 and was rebuilt in a new shape. Later repairs in the 1940s and 1950s gave it back its old look. Only some of the arches along the front are from mission days. Eight of them were rebuilt in 1989.

pages.subtitle: The twentieth California mission, begun as a place for the sick, on the homeland of the Coast Miwok people.
pages.founding_source_note: Toucan Valley fact card for Mission San Rafael Arcángel; Randall Milliken, National Park Service Coast Miwok report (December 1817).
pages.intro: Mission San Rafael Arcángel was the twentieth California mission. It was founded in 1817 on the homeland of the Coast Miwok people, north of San Francisco Bay. It began as a hospital for sick Native people from Mission Dolores, so it was named for the angel of healing. Nothing is left of the old mission buildings. The Coast Miwok people, though, are still here.
story_paragraphs: The Coast Miwok people have lived north of San Francisco Bay for a very long time. Their villages had names such as Olompali, Petaluma, and Olema. In 1579, sailors on an English ship wrote about meeting them. That is the oldest written record of the Coast Miwok.

When Mission Dolores was built in San Francisco, many Coast Miwok people were taken there. The weather at Dolores was cold, damp, and foggy. Sickness spread, and people who fell ill did not get better.

So, on December 14, 1817, Father Vicente de Sarría founded a new place across the bay, where it was sunny and warm. It was meant to be a hospital for Mission Dolores. A priest who knew something about medicine, Luis Gil y Taboada, was put in charge. The new mission was named for the Archangel Raphael, an angel known for good health and healing.
The sick did grow stronger there. In 1822, San Rafael became a full mission of its own. It was the twentieth California mission.

Many Coast Miwok people lived at San Rafael. From 1820 on, Pomo people from the north were brought there too, and soon more Pomo than Coast Miwok were being baptized. By 1828, more than 1,000 people lived at the mission.

Their tribe today, the Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria, says that the missions used its ancestors as workers. It says that the loss of their homelands, sickness from Europe, bad treatment, and enslavement caused their numbers to fall.

In 1834, San Rafael was taken away from the Church. General Mariano Vallejo was put in charge, and he moved the mission's animals and fruit trees to his own ranches. The mission was left empty in 1842, and in 1861 the old church was torn down.

In 1949, a small chapel was built near the old place to remember the mission. The Coast Miwok had no land of their own for many years. In 2000, the United States government once again recognized their tribe.

type_specific.native_peoples_and_history: This mission stands on the homeland of the Coast Miwok people. About 725 Coast Miwok people and about 780 Pomo people were baptized at San Rafael. Mission life brought forced work, strict rules, sickness, and the loss of land and freedom. When the mission closed, many Pomo families went back north. About 500 Native people settled on land at a place called Nicasio, but that land was taken from them bit by bit. A Coast Miwok man named Camilo Ynitia won a land grant at Olompali, the village of his people. A Coast Miwok man called Marin was baptized at Mission Dolores in 1801. The Marin Peninsula is named for him. Today, the Coast Miwok and Southern Pomo are joined in one tribe, the Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria. They have written a dictionary of the Coast Miwok language.
type_specific.mission_life: San Rafael was first of all a place to rest and get well. A cluster of Native houses stood around the main mission building. The sunny hills were good for farming and fruit trees. A priest named Juan Amorós led the mission after it became independent. Native people did the farming, herding, and building. The mission also helped Spain, and later Mexico, keep watch on the Russian traders who had a fort farther up the coast.
type_specific.architecture: Nothing is left of the first mission. Its simple church had no bell tower. The bells hung from a plain wooden frame outside the door. That church was torn down in 1861. The chapel you see today was built in 1949 as a copy, and it even faces a different way. The first church looked toward the bay, and the copy looks toward the hills. The copy has a star-shaped window over the door. People now think the real mission church almost surely did not have one. The idea came from an artist who drew the mission for a postcard long after it was gone.

pages.intro: Mission San Francisco Solano was the twenty-first and last California mission. Father José Altimira founded it in 1823 in the Sonoma Valley, on the homeland of the Coast Miwok people. It is the farthest north of all the missions, and the only one started after Mexico became free from Spain. It lasted just eleven years. Nearly 900 Native people are buried there.
story_paragraphs: The Sonoma Valley is the homeland of a group of Coast Miwok people called the Chocuyen. Other Native nations lived close by: the Patwin to the east, the Wappo to the north, and the Pomo beyond them.

In 1823, a young priest at Mission Dolores named José Altimira had a plan. He wanted to close Mission Dolores and Mission San Rafael and move everyone to a new mission in the warm Sonoma Valley. The governor liked the idea. He was worried about the Russian traders who had built a fort on the coast to the north.

On July 4, 1823, Father Altimira chose a place and blessed it. He started building before the head of the missions had said yes. In the end, the two older missions stayed open, and the new one became the twenty-first mission. It was named for Saint Francis Solano, a Spanish missionary who worked in Peru.

The first church was made of wood and mud. It was dedicated in 1824, and the first baptisms were held that day. In 1826, a fire destroyed it. A priest named Buenaventura Fortuni came to take Altimira's place, and he rebuilt with adobe.

People from many Native nations were baptized at the mission and used as its workers. By about 1832, nearly 1,000 Native people lived there. They farmed and herded on about 10,000 acres. Their tribe today says that the loss of their homelands, sickness, bad treatment, and enslavement caused their numbers to fall.

In 1834, after only eleven years, the government closed the mission. General Mariano Vallejo was put in charge. He laid out the town of Sonoma in front of the mission and moved many of the Native workers to his own ranches. The mission church soon fell down. In 1840, Vallejo built a small chapel for the town. That chapel is the one standing today.

In 1999, a monument was put up beside the chapel to honor the 896 Native people who are buried there. The Coast Miwok and Southern Pomo people are still here, joined together as the Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria.

type_specific.native_peoples_and_history: This mission was built on Coast Miwok land, but people from several nations were brought to it. Coast Miwok, Lake Miwok, Pomo, Patwin, and Wappo people were all baptized here. By the time the mission closed, most of the people there spoke Patwin, and the next largest group spoke Wappo. Mission life brought forced work, strict rules, sickness, and the loss of land and freedom. Some nations fought to keep their freedom. After 1835, soldiers rode out from Sonoma more than 100 times against the Wappo and their neighbors, who rose up again and again. Many Coast Miwok people who lived through the mission years went to work on General Vallejo's ranch. Today, the Coast Miwok and Southern Pomo are one tribe, the Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria. The United States recognized the tribe again in 2000.
type_specific.mission_life: In its few years, the mission grew crops and raised animals on about 10,000 acres. The Coast Miwok people who lived there were known as skilled weavers of cloth. When the first church was dedicated in 1824, the Russians at the fort sent gifts for it. Native people did the farming, herding, weaving, and building. After the mission closed, many of them had to work on the ranches of the men who now held the land.
type_specific.architecture: The long, low adobe building beside the chapel is the oldest building in Sonoma. It was the priests' house, and it is the only part of the mission that is left from mission days. It once had 27 rooms, and now it has five. Even this building was partly rebuilt after years of neglect. The chapel is not the mission church. General Vallejo built it in 1840, after the mission had closed. The great earthquake of 1906 badly damaged the buildings, and they were repaired between 1911 and 1913. Today the mission is part of a state historic park.
